messages.subject: NA MargLogLik and low BGammaHat
parts:
Hi,

I am fitting Bayesian RI-CLPMs with two variables (Enj, Eff, measured at 13 timepoints), two covariates (preTest, preEnj, measured at the beginning), two outcomes (postTest, game, measured at the end), and two dummy variables (3 groups: group0 is the reference of group1 and group2). The main research question is whether there are group differences on Enj, Eff, preTest, and game.

Some issues:
1.  MargLogLik value is NA. What does this mean and how should I proceed?
2.  BGammaHat .865, which is below .900, is quite different from BCFI .918. What could be the reason? How to increase the model fit? 
3. When looking at the output, are there any other things that I need to worry?

fit.RICLPMpoCogEnjEff <- '
# mediator
RIEnj ~ a1*group1 + a2*group2

# direct Effect
RIEff ~ c11*group1 + c12*group2
postTest ~ c21*group1 + c22*group2

messages.subject: Re: NA MargLogLik and low BGammaHat
parts:
Yuan

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

Hi,

I am fitting Bayesian RI-CLPMs with two variables (Enj, Eff, measured at 13 timepoints), two covariates (preTest, preEnj, measured at the beginning), two outcomes (postTest, game, measured at the end), and two dummy variables (3 groups: group0 is the reference of group1 and group2). The main research question is whether there are group differences on Enj, Eff, preTest, and game.

Some issues:
1.  MargLogLik value is NA. What does this mean and how should I proceed?

Yuan

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

1. 10000 is an overkill, if 1500 is enough to not get the ESS warnings you are fine. It would only be neccesary to have sucha a large sample for bayes factor estabilibility. But not for inferences etc

2. Yes, that is a warning not a problematic error

3. Sadly, that is a know problem with modification indices, they can take a while for large models, as it is estimating the lavaan indices 600 time for example. If R is still running I would let it run a for a bot. or you can increase thin so that it estimates it less times

out <- ppmc( fit.RICLPMpoCogEnjEff , thin=8, discFUN = discFUN)

as a last resort, you can run the model with lavaan and use its modification indices. They should not point to different parameters. Honetsly I am not sure what would be recommended as added parameters in this model with so many constraints

Yuan

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

In general should be colse to teach other of the model is the same. I would recommend to use the function sem and bsem to make sure that the same underlying constraints are used. For example, I am not sure you are running the same model with the argument fixed.x=T . Can check with fitMeasures of the blavaan object to have the same npar as the lavaan object

Also, these fit indices should be compare to the "normal" indices not the MLR ones

Since you are not actually sunning a multiple group model what matters more is the total sample

Even with models like this, would recommended to use priors less wide as the deafult ones

Didnt you say in an earlier post that the CFI was higher?

ML is not neccesarily the "correct" answer, so replicating them is not the objective of BSEM. Differences in the parameters can also be related to the unrealistic expectation of ML that your 130 sample is asymototically correct (equivalent to infinetly large)

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

In general should be colse to teach other of the model is the same. I would recommend to use the function sem and bsem to make sure that the same underlying constraints are used. For example, I am not sure you are running the same model with the argument fixed.x=T . Can check with fitMeasures of the blavaan object to have the same npar as the lavaan object

Also, these fit indices should be compare to the "normal" indices not the MLR ones

Since you are not actually sunning a multiple group model what matters more is the total sample

Even with models like this, would recommended to use priors less wide as the deafult ones

Didnt you say in an earlier post that the CFI was higher?

ML is not neccesarily the "correct" answer, so replicating them is not the objective of BSEM. Differences in the parameters can also be related to the unrealistic expectation of ML that your 130 sample is asymototically correct (equivalent to infinetly large)

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

Yuan

With MCMC the results will change a little bit between runs, due to MCMC error variability but should not change a lot.

The main difference is due to not be running the same model, as you have different number of parameters.

First, check between models and find what are the differences between them. Probably the fixed.x argument, you can give the same argument to blavaan and see if you get the same model. Can run it with very few iterations, just to see you have the right model.

Once you have the same model, I would recommend BSEM with weakly informative priors, these are good general applications for small sample sizes. Can get properly estimated models, that dont rely on the large sample assumption

In general should be colse to teach other of the model is the same. I would recommend to use the function sem and bsem to make sure that the same underlying constraints are used. For example, I am not sure you are running the same model with the argument fixed.x=T . Can check with fitMeasures of the blavaan object to have the same npar as the lavaan object

Also, these fit indices should be compare to the "normal" indices not the MLR ones

Since you are not actually sunning a multiple group model what matters more is the total sample

Even with models like this, would recommended to use priors less wide as the deafult ones

Didnt you say in an earlier post that the CFI was higher?

ML is not neccesarily the "correct" answer, so replicating them is not the objective of BSEM. Differences in the parameters can also be related to the unrealistic expectation of ML that your 130 sample is asymototically correct (equivalent to infinetly large)

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

Yuan

With MCMC the results will change a little bit between runs, due to MCMC error variability but should not change a lot.

The main difference is due to not be running the same model, as you have different number of parameters.

First, check between models and find what are the differences between them. Probably the fixed.x argument, you can give the same argument to blavaan and see if you get the same model. Can run it with very few iterations, just to see you have the right model.

Once you have the same model, I would recommend BSEM with weakly informative priors, these are good general applications for small sample sizes. Can get properly estimated models, that dont rely on the large sample assumption

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

With MCMC the results will change a little bit between runs, due to MCMC error variability but should not change a lot.

The main difference is due to not be running the same model, as you have different number of parameters.

First, check between models and find what are the differences between them. Probably the fixed.x argument, you can give the same argument to blavaan and see if you get the same model. Can run it with very few iterations, just to see you have the right model.

Once you have the same model, I would recommend BSEM with weakly informative priors, these are good general applications for small sample sizes. Can get properly estimated models, that dont rely on the large sample assumption

In general should be colse to teach other of the model is the same. I would recommend to use the function sem and bsem to make sure that the same underlying constraints are used. For example, I am not sure you are running the same model with the argument fixed.x=T . Can check with fitMeasures of the blavaan object to have the same npar as the lavaan object

Also, these fit indices should be compare to the "normal" indices not the MLR ones

Since you are not actually sunning a multiple group model what matters more is the total sample

Even with models like this, would recommended to use priors less wide as the deafult ones

Didnt you say in an earlier post that the CFI was higher?

ML is not neccesarily the "correct" answer, so replicating them is not the objective of BSEM. Differences in the parameters can also be related to the unrealistic expectation of ML that your 130 sample is asymototically correct (equivalent to infinetly large)

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

I dont usually use dummy variables as predictors like this. Because its hard to interpret what is the indirect effect and what is the indirect effect of the baseline groups. I would usually have group as a multiple group model, but that would be a moderation question, instead of mediation

These are the indirect effects of groups 2 compared to 0 group, and indirect of groups 3 to group 0. Not sure how meaningful this interpretation is?


Another option could be to include the 3 dummy code variables (no baseline group), and fixed the intercept of the outcome variables to 0. This way would estimate the paths for each group and you can define the difference between them. Havent use this approach for mediation, but I think it should work

With MCMC the results will change a little bit between runs, due to MCMC error variability but should not change a lot.

The main difference is due to not be running the same model, as you have different number of parameters.

Once you have the same model, I would recommend BSEM with weakly informative priors, these are good general applications for small sample sizes. Can get properly estimated models, that dont rely on the large sample assumption

In general should be colse to teach other of the model is the same. I would recommend to use the function sem and bsem to make sure that the same underlying constraints are used. For example, I am not sure you are running the same model with the argument fixed.x=T . Can check with fitMeasures of the blavaan object to have the same npar as the lavaan object

Also, these fit indices should be compare to the "normal" indices not the MLR ones

Since you are not actually sunning a multiple group model what matters more is the total sample

Even with models like this, would recommended to use priors less wide as the deafult ones

Didnt you say in an earlier post that the CFI was higher?

ML is not neccesarily the "correct" answer, so replicating them is not the objective of BSEM. Differences in the parameters can also be related to the unrealistic expectation of ML that your 130 sample is asymototically correct (equivalent to infinetly large)

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

I dont usually use dummy variables as predictors like this. Because its hard to interpret what is the indirect effect and what is the indirect effect of the baseline groups. I would usually have group as a multiple group model, but that would be a moderation question, instead of mediation

These are the indirect effects of groups 2 compared to 0 group, and indirect of groups 3 to group 0. Not sure how meaningful this interpretation is?


Another option could be to include the 3 dummy code variables (no baseline group), and fixed the intercept of the outcome variables to 0. This way would estimate the paths for each group and you can define the difference between them. Havent use this approach for mediation, but I think it should work

In general should be colse to teach other of the model is the same. I would recommend to use the function sem and bsem to make sure that the same underlying constraints are used. For example, I am not sure you are running the same model with the argument fixed.x=T . Can check with fitMeasures of the blavaan object to have the same npar as the lavaan object

Also, these fit indices should be compare to the "normal" indices not the MLR ones

Since you are not actually sunning a multiple group model what matters more is the total sample

Even with models like this, would recommended to use priors less wide as the deafult ones

Didnt you say in an earlier post that the CFI was higher?

ML is not neccesarily the "correct" answer, so replicating them is not the objective of BSEM. Differences in the parameters can also be related to the unrealistic expectation of ML that your 130 sample is asymototically correct (equivalent to infinetly large)

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

Including a dummy code for each group is possible in OLS regression, but not in analyses of covariance structure (SEM).  The dummy codes are multicollinear: 1 of them equals 1 minus the sum of the others.  However, a multigroup model would be conceptually equivalent to having a dummy code for each group.  The effect of the grouping variable is reflected by differences in intercepts across groups.  

https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00747

There are multiple indirect effects of a polytomous grouping variable, just like there are multiple direct effects (any pairwise comparison among the 3 groups).
You can find some lavaan example syntax in a power-analysis tutorial I coauthored:

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-022-01996-0

With MCMC the results will change a little bit between runs, due to MCMC error variability but should not change a lot.

The main difference is due to not be running the same model, as you have different number of parameters.

First, check between models and find what are the differences between them. Probably the fixed.x argument, you can give the same argument to blavaan and see if you get the same model. Can run it with very few iterations, just to see you have the right model.

Once you have the same model, I would recommend BSEM with weakly informative priors, these are good general applications for small sample sizes. Can get properly estimated models, that dont rely on the large sample assumption

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

  mods <- temp$mi

Hi Yuan

This is an interesting issue, that brings severals ideas. I havent read the full paper

1. Check what they mean "Dynamic", as there is a disagremment of what constitutes a dynamic model. For example, what Mplus calls DSEM is no consider dynamic by mnay people in the field (me included). But thet have taken the name, creating confusion. I wouldnt consider RI-CLPM as dynamic model. Can check the work of Ood , Voeckle, Chow, Moleenar, Diver
2. Can do a prior predictive simulation to see what distirbutions are the prior stating, I made a tutorial about this for blavaan https://ecmerkle.github.io/blavaan/articles/prior_pred_checks.html
3. I Think yo can use dpriors(normal(0, 0.5)) as with this you would have a prior with 95% between -1 and 1. In Stan the recommend to not have strint boundaries (unless is absolutely neccesary), as these priors are easier for the sampler

hist(rnorm(100000, mean=0, sd=1))
hist(rnorm(100000, mean=0, sd=.5))
qnorm(c(.025, .975), mean=0, sd=.5)
pnorm(c(-1,1), mean=0, sd=.5)

4. You can check the function blavpredict for possible doing posterior predictive checks. The problem, is that PPC are easier and make more sense when you have a single outcome item, while in SEM we usually have factors, multiple indicatros, multiple outcomes etc. So, what is a "meanigngful" outcome becomes a harder question to answer. Could be useful if there is a clear easy answer to it.

Hope this helps

I am exploring the influence of priors. Some follow-up questions for weakly informative priors:

e.g., NcNeish (2019; https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657 suggested:

"Two-Level Dynamic Structural Equation Models with Small Samples

assuming stationarity, the magnitude of the autoregressive inertia paths from the outcome at time t – 1 to the outcome at time t must fall between −1 and 1"

"Inertia Slope Variance.—The inertia slope of the outcome (y at time t) autoregressed on the outcome at the immediately preceding time (y at time t – 1) cannot exceed 1, provided that the assumption of stationarity has been met."

With MCMC the results will change a little bit between runs, due to MCMC error variability but should not change a lot.

The main difference is due to not be running the same model, as you have different number of parameters.

First, check between models and find what are the differences between them. Probably the fixed.x argument, you can give the same argument to blavaan and see if you get the same model. Can run it with very few iterations, just to see you have the right model.

Once you have the same model, I would recommend BSEM with weakly informative priors, these are good general applications for small sample sizes. Can get properly estimated models, that dont rely on the large sample assumption

In general should be colse to teach other of the model is the same. I would recommend to use the function sem and bsem to make sure that the same underlying constraints are used. For example, I am not sure you are running the same model with the argument fixed.x=T . Can check with fitMeasures of the blavaan object to have the same npar as the lavaan object

Also, these fit indices should be compare to the "normal" indices not the MLR ones

Since you are not actually sunning a multiple group model what matters more is the total sample

Even with models like this, would recommended to use priors less wide as the deafult ones

Didnt you say in an earlier post that the CFI was higher?

ML is not neccesarily the "correct" answer, so replicating them is not the objective of BSEM. Differences in the parameters can also be related to the unrealistic expectation of ML that your 130 sample is asymototically correct (equivalent to infinetly large)

some models with high number of constraints end up with issues of NA on on the margloglik, but this is not a problem in practice as it is only needed for bayes factor calculations (which I dont recommend)

About the gamma hat, remember that the cutoff of 0.9 is arbitrary and there is no reason to belief ot applies to all models/data, etc.

You can look at modification indices, but guven that you dont have an actual measurement model, might indicate to relase model constraints that could go agaiants the restrictions for theis model.

Another note, you dont need to save so many samples (1500 per chain), could probably do with 500

You can estimate posterior modifiction indices with this code and the ppmc function

### modification indices
discFUN <- list(mod.ind_mi = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  mods <- temp$mi
  names(mods) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(mods)
},mod.ind_sepc.all = function(object){
  temp <- modificationindices(object,free.remove = F)
  sepc.all <- temp$sepc.all
  names(sepc.all) <- paste0(temp$lhs,temp$op,temp$rhs)
  return(sepc.all )
}
)

#######
## PPMC - Modification indices
#######
out <- ppmc(bfit, thin=5, discFUN = discFUN)

### -MI
ss_mod_mi <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_mi", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]
### -SEPC
ss_mod_sepc <- summary(out, prob=.9, discFUN = "mod.ind_sepc.all", sort.by="Median", decreasing=T)[1:5,]

parts:
Yuanyuan,

A couple additions to Mauricio's response:

I imagine that you have multiple slopes in your model, and the dpriors() thing sets a prior distribution for all slopes. So you might want to use prior() inside the model specification syntax. See:

https://ecmerkle.github.io/blavaan/articles/prior.html#individual-parameters

About ppmc() taking a long time: this partly depends on your model. If you have many columns in your data and/or missing data, it will take longer. I believe that future::plan("multicore") can help here (or "multisession" on windows), but it might still take awhile.

Ed

Hi Mauricio,
>
I am exploring the influence of priors. Some follow-up questions for
> weakly informative priors:
> 1. Specific priors for RI-CLPMs: do you have any recommendations on
> the values? 
> e.g., NcNeish
> (2019; [https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657) suggested:

> "Two-Level Dynamic Structural Equation Models with Small Samples
> assuming stationarity, the magnitude of the autoregressive inertia
> paths from the outcome at time t – 1 to the outcome at time t must
> fall between −1 and 1"
> "Inertia Slope Variance.—The inertia slope of the outcome (y at time
> t) autoregressed on the outcome at the immediately preceding time (y
> at time t – 1) cannot exceed 1, provided that the assumption of
> stationarity has been met."

>  *
>  *

> 2. How to set these specific priors in blavaan?
> E.g., dp=dpriors(XX) , to specify Inertia Slope Variance (0,1)
> and autoregressive effect (-1, 1), what should XX be replaced?
>
3. How to do the posterior predictive checking?

> AFIs <- ppmc(fit.RICLPMEnjEff, thin = 10, fit.measures =

> summary(AFIs) 
> Can we do something in blavaan that is similar to posterior
> predictive checking on the following website?

>
Best,

在2023年8月20日星期日 UTC+2 18:37:21<Ed Merkle> 写道：

Yuanyuan,

A couple additions to Mauricio's response:

I imagine that you have multiple slopes in your model, and the dpriors() thing sets a prior distribution for all slopes. So you might want to use prior() inside the model specification syntax. See:

https://ecmerkle.github.io/blavaan/articles/prior.html#individual-parameters

About ppmc() taking a long time: this partly depends on your model. If you have many columns in your data and/or missing data, it will take longer. I believe that future::plan("multicore") can help here (or "multisession" on windows), but it might still take awhile.

Ed


On Wed, 2023-08-16 at 07:44 -0700, Yuanyuan Hu wrote:


Hi Mauricio,
>
I am exploring the influence of priors. Some follow-up questions for
> weakly informative priors:
> 1. Specific priors for RI-CLPMs: do you have any recommendations on
> the values? 
> e.g., NcNeish
> (2019; [https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657) suggested:

> "Two-Level Dynamic Structural Equation Models with Small Samples
> assuming stationarity, the magnitude of the autoregressive inertia

在2023年8月20日星期日 UTC+2 18:37:21<Ed Merkle> 写道：

Yuanyuan,

A couple additions to Mauricio's response:

I imagine that you have multiple slopes in your model, and the dpriors() thing sets a prior distribution for all slopes. So you might want to use prior() inside the model specification syntax. See:

https://ecmerkle.github.io/blavaan/articles/prior.html#individual-parameters

About ppmc() taking a long time: this partly depends on your model. If you have many columns in your data and/or missing data, it will take longer. I believe that future::plan("multicore") can help here (or "multisession" on windows), but it might still take awhile.

Ed

Hi Mauricio,
>
I am exploring the influence of priors. Some follow-up questions for
> weakly informative priors:
> 1. Specific priors for RI-CLPMs: do you have any recommendations on
> the values? 
> e.g., NcNeish
> (2019; [https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657) suggested:

> "Two-Level Dynamic Structural Equation Models with Small Samples
> assuming stationarity, the magnitude of the autoregressive inertia
> paths from the outcome at time t – 1 to the outcome at time t must
> fall between −1 and 1"
> "Inertia Slope Variance.—The inertia slope of the outcome (y at time
> t) autoregressed on the outcome at the immediately preceding time (y
> at time t – 1) cannot exceed 1, provided that the assumption of
> stationarity has been met."
>  *
>  *
> 2. How to set these specific priors in blavaan?
> E.g., dp=dpriors(XX) , to specify Inertia Slope Variance (0,1)

3. How to do the posterior predictive checking?

> AFIs <- ppmc(fit.RICLPMEnjEff, thin = 10, fit.measures =

Yuanyuan,

A couple additions to Mauricio's response:

I imagine that you have multiple slopes in your model, and the dpriors() thing sets a prior distribution for all slopes. So you might want to use prior() inside the model specification syntax. See:

https://ecmerkle.github.io/blavaan/articles/prior.html#individual-parameters

About ppmc() taking a long time: this partly depends on your model. If you have many columns in your data and/or missing data, it will take longer. I believe that future::plan("multicore") can help here (or "multisession" on windows), but it might still take awhile.

Ed

> (2019; [https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657) suggested:

> assuming stationarity, the magnitude of the autoregressive inertia

> fall between −1 and 1"
> "Inertia Slope Variance.—The inertia slope of the outcome (y at time
> t) autoregressed on the outcome at the immediately preceding time (y
> at time t – 1) cannot exceed 1, provided that the assumption of
> stationarity has been met."

messages.subject: Re: NA MargLogLik and low BGammaHat
parts:
Yuan

Actually I think it is easier with multiple groups, but not with the same logic of testing as in frequentist methods. I guess you are thinking on adding the inequality constraints and then compared the models and see how much "better" a model with or without the constraints. This is the same logic as in frequentist methods.

But within Bayesian, we actually dont need to use constraints for hypothesis. Once you have a multiple group model, you can extract the posterior distributions of the groups means, and estimate the posterior distribution of the difference between them (leading to ordered constraints of how much "larger" is one group over another). The objective being to estimate proper distributions for the hypothesis of interest, and the "hypothesis" is done by inter[reting these posterior distributions

take care

Yuan

Actually I think it is easier with multiple groups, but not with the same logic of testing as in frequentist methods. I guess you are thinking on adding the inequality constraints and then compared the models and see how much "better" a model with or without the constraints. This is the same logic as in frequentist methods.

But within Bayesian, we actually dont need to use constraints for hypothesis. Once you have a multiple group model, you can extract the posterior distributions of the groups means, and estimate the posterior distribution of the difference between them (leading to ordered constraints of how much "larger" is one group over another). The objective being to estimate proper distributions for the hypothesis of interest, and the "hypothesis" is done by inter[reting these posterior distributions

take care

Actually I think it is easier with multiple groups, but not with the same logic of testing as in frequentist methods. I guess you are thinking on adding the inequality constraints and then compared the models and see how much "better" a model with or without the constraints. This is the same logic as in frequentist methods.

But within Bayesian, we actually dont need to use constraints for hypothesis. Once you have a multiple group model, you can extract the posterior distributions of the groups means, and estimate the posterior distribution of the difference between them (leading to ordered constraints of how much "larger" is one group over another). The objective being to estimate proper distributions for the hypothesis of interest, and the "hypothesis" is done by inter[reting these posterior distributions

take care

Actually I think it is easier with multiple groups, but not with the same logic of testing as in frequentist methods. I guess you are thinking on adding the inequality constraints and then compared the models and see how much "better" a model with or without the constraints. This is the same logic as in frequentist methods.

But within Bayesian, we actually dont need to use constraints for hypothesis. Once you have a multiple group model, you can extract the posterior distributions of the groups means, and estimate the posterior distribution of the difference between them (leading to ordered constraints of how much "larger" is one group over another). The objective being to estimate proper distributions for the hypothesis of interest, and the "hypothesis" is done by inter[reting these posterior distributions

take care
